answers.explanation: The formulas and predicate vocabulary are fixed; the unary expansions vary. Each expansion yields an interpreted graph, so one input can have several outputs.
A homomorphism maps vertices while preserving edges; it does not redefine adjacency by arbitrary FO formulas.
Minor operations delete or contract edges and vertices; an FO transduction can also create edges.
An isomorphism preserves the whole adjacency relation bijectively. Here both the domain and adjacency may change.

answers.text: A deterministic interpretation of the uncoloured graph alone.
answers.explanation: The arbitrary unary expansions are extra choices, so the output is not determined by the uncoloured input alone.

answers.text: A vertex-colouring operation with adjacency unchanged.
answers.explanation: Colouring is only the preparatory step; the formulas can also change edges and select a domain.

answers.text: An arbitrary MSO transduction requiring vertex-set quantifiers in its defining formulas.
answers.explanation: The defining formulas here are first-order. Unary parameters do not make their quantifiers second-order.

answers.text: A two-dimensional interpretation whose output vertices must be ordered pairs.

answers.text: A copying transduction with an unbounded input-dependent number of copies.

questions.prompt: Let $G$ be a finite simple graph and $G^+$ a unary expansion of $G$. How does a non-copying FO transduction with domain formula $\delta$ and symmetric, irreflexive edge formula $\varphi$ construct an output graph $H$?

answers.explanation: Evaluate both fixed formulas in the expanded input. The domain formula selects output vertices; the edge formula determines adjacency between them.

answers.text: $V(H)=V(G)$; retain exactly the original edges, regardless of $\delta$ and $\varphi$.
answers.explanation: This ignores both defining formulas and cannot describe a general transduction.

answers.text: $V(H)=\{v\in V(G):G^+\models\varphi(v,v)\}$; for $u,v\in V(H)$, adjacency is determined by $\delta(u)\land\delta(v)$.
answers.explanation: The edge formula is irreflexive, so its diagonal is empty. The roles of the domain and edge formulas are reversed.

answers.text: $V(H)=E(G)$; join two output vertices when the corresponding input edges meet.
answers.explanation: That describes the line-graph construction, not this one-dimensional vertex-domain definition.

answers.text: $V(H)=\{v\in V(G):G^+\models\delta(v)\}$; keep only input edges that also satisfy $\varphi$.
answers.explanation: An FO edge formula may create an edge that was absent from the input. Intersecting with the old edge set is an extra restriction.
Quantified variables of the edge formula range over the input structure. Deleting unselected witnesses first can change its truth.

answers.text: $V(H)=\{v\in V(G):G^+\models\delta(v)\}$; evaluate $\varphi$ after forgetting all added predicates.
answers.explanation: The edge formula is allowed to use those unary predicates.

answers.text: Select vertices by $\delta$, but for $u,v\in V(H)$ require $\varphi(u,v)$ in every unary expansion of $G$.
answers.explanation: Each individual expansion can produce its own output. Taking the intersection over all expansions changes the operation.

answers.text: Select vertices by $\delta$, but choose a separate unary expansion for each pair $u,v\in V(H)$.
answers.explanation: One expansion must determine the entire output graph, not a different expansion for each potential edge.

answers.text: Select vertices by $\delta$, but evaluate $\varphi$ in the output graph $H$ itself.
answers.explanation: The formulas are evaluated in the input expansion. Evaluating them recursively in the output is not this definition.

questions.prompt: For graph classes $\mathcal C,\mathcal D$, what does $\mathcal D\subseteq T(\mathcal C)$ require of a single fixed FO transduction $T$?

answers.text: One fixed finite vocabulary and fixed formulas work for every $H\in\mathcal D$; the chosen $G\in\mathcal C$ and its colouring may depend on $H$.
answers.explanation: Uniformity concerns the recipe, not the input graph or colouring. Every target must occur among the outputs of that one recipe.

answers.text: Every $G\in\mathcal C$ must produce every $H\in\mathcal D$.
answers.explanation: Class transducibility only requires some suitable input for each target.

answers.text: One finite $G\in\mathcal C$ must produce all graphs of every order in $\mathcal D$.
answers.explanation: A fixed finite input has bounded output size. The input is allowed to vary with the target.

answers.text: The defining formula may be chosen separately for each target $H\in\mathcal D$.
answers.explanation: That discards the fixed-recipe requirement.

answers.text: The formulas are fixed, but the number of unary predicates may grow with the target.
answers.explanation: The finite predicate vocabulary is also part of the fixed transduction.

answers.text: The vocabulary is fixed, but quantifier rank may grow through a new formula for each target.
answers.explanation: A fixed transduction uses fixed formulas, hence a fixed quantifier rank.

answers.text: The recipe must generate exactly $\mathcal D$ and no additional outputs.
answers.explanation: The definition asks for containment in the outputs, not equality.

answers.text: Each target uses one recipe for vertices and unrelated input graphs for its individual edges.
answers.explanation: The whole output is interpreted in a single expanded input graph.

answers.text: The unary predicates must be FO-definable in the uncoloured input.
answers.explanation: They are arbitrary unary parameters, not predicates required to be definable without parameters.

answers.text: The formulas and one fixed colouring assignment must work unchanged on all input graphs.
answers.explanation: The formulas are uniform, but colour assignments are chosen separately on each input vertex set.

questions.prompt: For a finite simple input graph $G$, how is a $k$-copy operation, with $k$ a positive integer, used in an FO transduction?

answers.text: Use a fixed $k$, distinguish the copies, and link corresponding copies of each original vertex before the fixed FO interpretation.
answers.explanation: Copying supplies finitely many tagged copies and a correspondence relation. The constant and interpretation belong to the transduction, not to individual inputs.

answers.text: Take $|V(G)|$ copies and choose new defining formulas for each input.
answers.explanation: Both an input-dependent copy number and input-dependent formulas violate the fixed-transduction convention.

answers.text: Replace every vertex by all subsets of the input vertex set.
answers.explanation: A fixed-copy operation gives only a constant-factor increase, not a powerset domain.

answers.text: Contract every connected component before interpreting the graph.
answers.explanation: Copying duplicates vertices; it is not a component quotient.

answers.text: Take a fixed number of untagged copies and erase which vertices correspond.
answers.explanation: The standard copying structure supplies copy tags and the correspondence relation for the formulas to use.

answers.text: Allow arbitrarily many copies as long as the edge formula is fixed.
answers.explanation: The copy number itself must also be fixed.

answers.text: Use a fixed number of copies, but require the output to contain every copied vertex.
answers.explanation: The subsequent interpretation may select a smaller domain.

answers.text: Use a fixed number of copies, but forbid formulas from relating different copies.
answers.explanation: The correspondence relation and copy tags are supplied precisely so cross-copy relationships can be defined.

answers.text: Use a fixed number of copies, identified into one equivalence class per original vertex before any formula is evaluated.
answers.explanation: That collapses the copies before interpretation. Standard copying retains the distinct copies as available elements.

answers.text: Use a fixed number of copies only when all unary parameters are already definable in the original graph.
answers.explanation: Arbitrary finitely many unary parameters are allowed; definability in the original graph is not required.

questions.prompt: A class of finite simple graphs $\mathcal C$ cannot produce every finite simple graph by any one fixed FO transduction, even with arbitrary finitely many unary vertex predicates. What is this property called?

answers.explanation: The forbidden encoding is a single uniform recipe for all finite graphs. Unary expansions account for the word “monadic”.
Bounded clique-width implies this property, but its definition uses labelled graph expressions and is stronger.
Twin-width is defined by contraction sequences. Monadic dependence also includes classes with unbounded twin-width.
Shrubdepth requires uniformly bounded tree-model height and colour count, a stronger condition.
Independence is the opposite: some fixed transduction does encode all finite graphs.
Stability forbids transducing all half-graphs, not merely all finite graphs; it is stronger.
Nowhere denseness is a sparse structural property; monadic dependence also permits arbitrarily large cliques.
Bounded merge-width controls each radius by a constant. Monadic dependence need only yield almost bounded merge-width.

answers.text: Bounded VC-dimension of the adjacency relation alone.
answers.explanation: Monadic dependence controls every fixed FO encoding after unary expansions, not only raw adjacency.

answers.text: Exclusion of one finite graph as an induced subgraph.
answers.explanation: An induced-subgraph exclusion alone does not prevent logical encodings of all graphs.

questions.prompt: Let $\mathcal C$ be a class of finite simple graphs and $\mathcal G$ the class of all such graphs. Let $T$ range over fixed FO transductions with unary parameters; $T(\mathcal C)$ is the union of its outputs on members of $\mathcal C$. Which condition defines monadic dependence of $\mathcal C$?

answers.text: $\forall T\;\exists H\in\mathcal G:\ H\notin T(\mathcal C)$.
answers.explanation: Every fixed recipe misses at least one finite graph. The graph it misses may depend on the recipe.

answers.text: $\exists T\;\forall H\in\mathcal G:\ H\in T(\mathcal C)$.
answers.explanation: This is monadic independence, the negation of dependence.

answers.text: $\forall T\;\forall H\in\mathcal G:\ H\notin T(\mathcal C)$.
answers.explanation: This forbids even trivial outputs; dependence only requires each recipe to miss some graph.

answers.text: $\exists T\;\exists H\in\mathcal G:\ H\notin T(\mathcal C)$.
answers.explanation: One weak transduction missing a graph says nothing about another transduction encoding all graphs.

answers.text: $\exists H\in\mathcal G\;\forall T:\ H\notin T(\mathcal C)$.
answers.explanation: This swaps the quantifiers. For example, large cliques can encode any one fixed finite graph using finitely many colours tailored to that graph.

answers.text: $\forall H\in\mathcal G\;\exists T:\ H\notin T(\mathcal C)$.
answers.explanation: Choosing a deliberately unhelpful transduction separately for each target does not rule out a universal encoding.

answers.text: $\forall T\;\exists G\in\mathcal C\;\exists H\in\mathcal G:\ H\notin T(G)$.
answers.explanation: Failure on one input is insufficient: the target might be produced from another input in the class.

answers.text: $\forall T\;\exists H\in\mathcal G:\ H\notin T(\mathcal C)$, but only for transductions without unary parameters.
answers.explanation: Removing unary parameters weakens the test. Monadic dependence explicitly allows arbitrary finite unary expansions.

answers.text: $\forall T\;\exists H\in\mathcal G:\ H\notin T(\mathcal C)$, but only for quantifier-free edge formulas.
answers.explanation: All first-order formulas must be considered, not just quantifier-free ones.

answers.text: $\forall G\in\mathcal C\;\forall T\;\exists H\in\mathcal G:\ H\notin T(G)$.
answers.explanation: Every fixed finite input has bounded output size. This holds even for the class of all finite graphs.

questions.prompt: Let $\mathcal C,\mathcal D$ be classes of finite simple graphs, with $\mathcal C$ monadically dependent and $\mathcal D\subseteq T(\mathcal C)$ for a fixed FO transduction $T$. What follows?

answers.text: $\mathcal D$ is monadically dependent: a universal encoding from $\mathcal D$ would compose with $T$ to give one from $\mathcal C$.
answers.explanation: FO transductions compose. If a transduction of the output class encoded all graphs, the composition would contradict dependence of the input class.

answers.text: $\mathcal D$ must be monadically independent, because a transduction adds arbitrary colours.
answers.explanation: Arbitrary colours are already allowed in the definition of monadic dependence.

answers.text: $\mathcal D$ must have bounded shrubdepth, regardless of $\mathcal C$.
answers.explanation: The identity transduction on all paths disproves this: paths are monadically dependent but have unbounded shrubdepth.

answers.text: $\mathcal D$ must have bounded clique-width, regardless of $\mathcal C$.
answers.explanation: The identity on planar grids disproves this: they are dependent but have unbounded clique-width.

answers.text: Dependence follows only when $T$ is injective on isomorphism classes.
answers.explanation: The composition argument needs no injectivity.

answers.text: Dependence follows only when $T$ never changes adjacency.
answers.explanation: Composition works for arbitrary allowed edge formulas, including complementation.

answers.text: Dependence follows only when $\mathcal D=T(\mathcal C)$.
answers.explanation: A subclass of a dependent class is dependent; containment is sufficient.

answers.text: Dependence follows only when $\mathcal C$ is closed under arbitrary subgraphs.
answers.explanation: The composition argument requires no subgraph-closure assumption.

answers.text: Dependence follows only when each input has a unique output under $T$.
answers.explanation: Set-valued transductions still compose; unary choices can be encoded together.

answers.text: Dependence follows only when $T$ has quantifier-free formulas.
answers.explanation: Fixed first-order formulas are closed under the substitutions used in composition.

questions.prompt: Fix an integer $k\ge2$; label indices $i,j$ range over $\{1,\ldots,k\}$. Which operation is permitted by a standard $k$-expression for clique-width?

answers.text: For $i\ne j$, add every missing edge between the current label-$i$ and label-$j$ vertices.
answers.explanation: A join acts uniformly on two distinct label classes. It adds edges and leaves existing edges in place.

answers.text: Delete an arbitrary existing edge while preserving all labels.
answers.explanation: Edge deletion is not a primitive operation of a clique-width expression.

answers.text: Identify any two vertices of the same label.
answers.explanation: Clique-width expressions build graphs without contracting vertices.

answers.text: Add just one chosen edge between two otherwise indistinguishable labelled vertices.
answers.explanation: A join treats entire label classes uniformly, not chosen individual vertices within them.

answers.text: Complement adjacency between two label classes in one primitive step.
answers.explanation: The join adds all missing edges; it does not toggle or remove existing edges.

answers.text: Relabel one chosen vertex in a label class while leaving the others unchanged.
answers.explanation: The relabelling operation changes every vertex carrying the source label.

answers.text: Create an arbitrary nonempty labelled graph as a single atomic expression.
answers.explanation: The atomic expressions create single labelled vertices.

answers.text: Apply a same-label join $\eta_{i,i}$ as a primitive operation.
answers.explanation: The standard definition requires distinct labels. Same-label joins belong to a modified convention.

answers.text: Give one vertex several simultaneous construction labels.
answers.explanation: In the standard definition every vertex carries exactly one label at each stage.

answers.text: Join only across the two operands of a union, using their origin as an extra test.
answers.explanation: A standard clique-width join sees current labels, not which union operand a vertex came from; that origin-sensitive primitive is NLC-style.
